widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_panel(seed, n=400, p=10):
    """n share-months in month order, p features (z-scores), next-month return in %.
    Only the first three features matter: 0.6, 0.4 and -0.3 per unit."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, p))
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, 0.4, -0.3]
    y = 0.5 + X @ beta + 3.0 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    return X, y

screens.title: The algebra under `.fit`
screens.prose: `.fit` solves the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$ from the least squares course, with a column of ones in $\mathbf{X}$. It stores the intercept in `model.intercept_` and the slopes in `model.coef_`. Check that by hand.
screens.question: Complete `normal_eq_coef` so it returns the slopes only, to match `model.coef_`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def normal_eq_coef(X, y):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
    beta = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y)
    return np.round(beta[1:], 6)

It will explain about 79% of next month's returns

options.text: It is a little optimistic: expect about 0.7 on new rows

options.text: Being positive, it proves the model beats the mean
options.why: OLS with an intercept can never score below 0 on its own training rows. A positive training $R^2$ proves nothing.

screens.title: More features than rows
screens.prose: Now give the 40 features only 30 training rows. The normal equations have 41 unknowns and 30 rows of data, so $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ cannot be inverted.
screens.question: What does `LinearRegression().fit` do here?

options.text: Returns one of infinitely many exact fits, the one with the smallest coefficients; train MSE is 0
Raises an error, because $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular
options.why: You expected it to invert $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$. scikit-learn uses a least squares solver that never inverts it, so it returns an answer.

options.text: Drops 11 features so the rest can be fitted
options.why: You expected it to choose features for you. OLS never drops a column; it keeps all 40.

options.text: Falls back to predicting the training mean
options.why: You expected a safe fallback. It fits the 30 rows exactly instead.

With more unknowns than equations, an exact fit is easy and not unique.
Many $\boldsymbol\beta$ give zero training error. The solver returns the one with the smallest $\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert$.

feedback.correct: Train MSE is 0 and the coefficients are one choice among infinitely many.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count unknowns against rows.

explain.text: Train MSE is $2 \times 10^{-29}$: zero up to rounding. On the 2,000 test rows the MSE is 23.98, about double the baseline's 12.15. Lesson 7 adds a penalty that makes the answer unique and far less wild.

screens.title: Why only the test score can go negative
screens.prose: Training $R^2$ for OLS with an intercept is never below 0. Test $R^2$ can be. Put the argument in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: OLS chooses $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ to make the training SSE as small as possible over every $\boldsymbol\beta$
The mean-only model, intercept $\bar y_{\text{train}}$ and every slope 0, is one candidate, so $\text{SSE}_{\text{train}} \le \text{SST}_{\text{train}}$
The test rows played no part in choosing $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, so nothing caps $\text{MSE}_{\text{model}}$ at $\text{MSE}_{\text{baseline}}$, and $R^2_{\text{test}}$ can be negative

hints.text: Start from what OLS does on the training rows.
The mean-only model is a special $\boldsymbol\beta$ that OLS also considered.
Minimum, then the candidate, then the training bound, then why the bound fails on test rows.

feedback.correct: The bound comes from the minimisation, and the minimisation only saw the training rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with what OLS minimises, and end with the test rows.

byKey.test: The test line explains why the bound fails. It needs the training bound first.
byKey.pos: The bound on $R^2_{\text{train}}$ needs the comparison with the mean-only model first.

explain.text: OLS beat every $\boldsymbol\beta$ on the training rows, the mean-only one included. That guarantee says nothing about rows it never saw. The colleague's test score, −0.95 in scikit-learn, is what happens when the fit chased noise.

screens.title: The honest score
screens.prose: Fit on the training rows, then score on held-out rows against the forecast you could have made without features: $$R^2_{\text{test}} = 1 - \frac{\text{MSE}_{\text{test}}(\text{model})}{\text{MSE}_{\text{test}}(\bar y_{\text{train}})}.$$ scikit-learn's `model.score(X_test, y_test)` uses the test rows' own mean instead. The difference is usually small.
screens.question: A model's test MSE is 12.9 and the baseline's is 12.3. What is $R^2_{\text{test}}$?

options.why: You subtracted the wrong way round. The model's error is larger, so it removed less than nothing.
That is the ratio of the two MSEs. $R^2_{\text{test}}$ is 1 minus it.
You floored it at 0. Test $R^2$ has no floor: a worse-than-baseline model scores below 0.

hints.text: Divide the model's MSE by the baseline's.

feedback.correct: Below 0: the model forecast worse than the training mean.

explain.text: $1 - 12.9/12.3 = -0.049$. A negative test $R^2$ is a verdict, not an error: drop the model or the features that hurt it.

screens.title: A cross-sectional return model
screens.prose: A desk regresses next-month return on five features over 400 share-months, monthly returns with a spread of about 8%. It trains on the first 300 rows and tests on the last 100.
screens.question: What is the model's test $R^2$, in per cent?

widget.label: Test R squared in per cent

hints.text: Use the test column only.
Divide the model's test MSE by the baseline's.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1 - 65.76/67.04$ and give it in per cent.

byKey.train: That is the training $R^2$. The question asks about the 100 test rows.
byKey.ratio: That ratio is the error left. Subtract it from 1.

explain.text: $1 - 65.76/67.04 = 0.0191$, about 1.9%. Large studies of monthly stock returns report out-of-sample $R^2$ around 1% or less, so this is what a real signal looks like. Spread over hundreds of shares a month, a 2% edge can still pay.

ideas: `LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)` is the OLS you know; only the held-out rows can say how good it is.
The fair rival is the training mean; test $R^2$ is the share of its error the model removes, and it can be negative.
Extra columns always lower training error; past a point they raise test error, and with more columns than rows OLS fits the noise exactly.

formula.name: Test $R^2$
formula.note: On monthly returns, 1% to 2% is a real signal.

summary.trap: A training score, `model.score(X_train, y_train)`, grades the model on rows it has already seen; it says nothing about skill.

quiz.prose: A column in `X_train` is 1.0 on every row. You fit `LinearRegression()` with its usual intercept.
quiz.question: What coefficient does that column get?

options.text: 0: once each column is centred it is all zeros, and the solver gives it nothing
The intercept's value, since it does the intercept's job
options.why: You gave it the intercept's role. The intercept is fitted separately, so this column adds nothing and gets 0.

options.text: An error, because the column is collinear with the intercept
options.why: You expected a singular-matrix error. scikit-learn's least squares solver returns the minimum-norm answer instead.

options.text: A huge number, because the variance is zero
options.why: You expected the zero spread to blow up the estimate. The solver sets it to 0 rather than divide by zero.

feedback.correct: A constant column carries no information about which share does better.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what is left of the column after its mean is taken off.

byKey.err: You expected an error. The solver quietly returns 0 for that column.

explain.text: scikit-learn centres every column before fitting; a constant column becomes all zeros. Its coefficient is 0 and predictions are unchanged. Drop such columns anyway: they only hide mistakes.

quiz.prose: You add one column of pure random numbers to an OLS model and refit.
quiz.question: What happens to training MSE and test MSE?

options.text: Training MSE cannot rise; test MSE usually rises a little
Both fall, because the model has more to work with
options.why: You trusted the training error. The new column fits noise in the training rows, which does not repeat.

options.text: Training MSE rises, because the column is noise
options.why: OLS could set the new coefficient to 0 and keep the old fit, so training MSE cannot rise.

options.text: Neither changes, because OLS sets its coefficient to 0
options.why: OLS gives it whatever slope lowers training SSE, which is almost never exactly 0.

feedback.correct: More columns only ever help on the rows they were fitted to.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. OLS can always ignore a column, but it rarely does.

explain.text: The old fit is still available, so training SSE cannot rise, and the new slope chases noise to lower it a little. That chasing costs on new rows.

quiz.question: What is the model's test $R^2$?

feedback.correct: Negative: the features made forecasts worse.

byKey.flip: You divided the baseline by the model. The model's MSE goes on top.
byKey.pos: You dropped the sign. The model's error is larger, so $R^2_{\text{test}}$ is below 0.

explain.text: $8.6/8.0 = 1.075$, so $R^2_{\text{test}} = -0.075$. The model is 7.5% worse than using no features at all.

quiz.prose: The baseline forecast for every test row is the mean of the **training** returns.
quiz.question: Why not use the mean of the test returns?

options.text: It is only known after the test period, so no real forecaster could use it
The test set is smaller, so its mean is too noisy
options.why: Size is not the issue. Even a large test set's mean uses returns that had not happened yet.

options.text: The two means are always equal
options.why: They differ; in panel 2 the training mean is 0.84% and the test mean is different.

options.text: It is a convention with no effect on the score
options.why: It has an effect: the test mean always scores at least as well as any other constant on those rows, which flatters the baseline.

feedback.correct: A baseline must be a forecast you could have made at the time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when each mean becomes known.

explain.text: A fair test pits the model against a rival that knows no more than it did. The training mean is that rival; the test mean peeks at the answers.
